proposed_title: U.S. B-2 bombers strike three Iranian nuclear sites in Operation Midnight Hammer
proposed_description_short: U.S. B-2 bombers strike three Iranian nuclear sites in Operation Midnight Hammer
proposed_description_medium: U.S. forces carried out Operation Midnight Hammer on June 22, 2025, striking nuclear facilities at Natanz, Fordow, and Isfahan. U.S. Strategic Command described the operation; later reporting on a U.S. assessment said only one of the three sites was destroyed. The evidence supports strikes on the facilities, not a categorical claim that Natanz was destroyed.
proposed_description_long:
On June 22, 2025, U.S. forces carried out Operation Midnight Hammer, using B-2 bombers to strike Iranian nuclear facilities at Natanz, Fordow, and Isfahan, according to U.S. Strategic Command. The operation was a major military action against Iran's nuclear program. The frozen record gives June 13 as the event date and says Natanz was destroyed, but the operation occurred on June 22 and the sources distinguish strikes from later damage assessments.

NBC News later reported on a U.S. assessment that found the strikes destroyed only one of the three targeted sites, challenging claims that all three were destroyed. The cited reporting therefore supports saying the sites were struck, while the extent of damage—especially at Natanz—should be attributed to the relevant assessment rather than stated as settled fact. A claim that Natanz was destroyed requires evidence specific to that facility and a clear account of the assessment's timing.

frozen_original.title: Iran's Natanz Nuclear Facility Destroyed by US B-2 Bombers
frozen_original.synopsis: US B-2 Spirit stealth bombers delivered precision strikes that destroyed Iran's Natanz nuclear enrichment complex in June 2025, the centerpiece of Iran's nuclear program and a site that had been under IAEA monitoring. The Natanz facility housed thousands of centrifuges for uranium enrichment and had been hardened and expanded in the years following Trump's 2018 JCPOA withdrawal. The destruction of Natanz represented the most consequential US military strike since the 2003 invasion of Iraq. IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi condemned the strike as a violation of international law regarding safeguarded nuclear facilities, and the UN Security Council convened an emergency session. Russia and China condemned the attack in the strongest terms.

proposed_title: Trump publicly asks Russia to find Clinton's deleted emails on July 27, 2016
proposed_description_short: Trump publicly asks Russia to find Clinton's deleted emails on July 27, 2016
proposed_description_medium: On July 27, 2016, Donald Trump publicly said, 'Russia, if you're listening,' and asked Russia to find emails Hillary Clinton had deleted. The Mueller report says Russian military intelligence targeted Clinton campaign personal-office accounts within about five hours. The sources do not support the frozen title's claim that Trump made the request 21 times.
proposed_description_long:
During a July 27, 2016 news conference, Donald Trump publicly said, “Russia, if you're listening,” and called on Russia to find emails Hillary Clinton had deleted. The Special Counsel's Mueller report states that within approximately five hours, Russian military intelligence officers began targeting email accounts connected to Clinton's personal office. The report documents the chronology between Trump's public statement and the GRU activity.

The frozen title says Trump asked Russia for dirt on Clinton 21 times. The sources reviewed do not establish that count or show 21 separate requests. The event supported here is one widely reported public statement and the subsequent timing of the GRU targeting as described by the Special Counsel. The chronology does not by itself establish that the statement caused the operation or prove coordination. The DOJ indictment offers additional allegations about Russian activity, but its allegations should not be described as a judicial finding.

frozen_original.title: Trump Asked Russia for Dirt on Clinton 21 Times
frozen_original.synopsis: According to a Senate Intelligence Committee analysis of Trump's public statements, he directly or indirectly solicited Russian assistance against Hillary Clinton approximately 21 separate times during the 2016 campaign. Most notoriously, on July 27, 2016, Trump publicly called on Russia to find Clinton's deleted emails — a request that Russian intelligence units later attempted to fulfill within hours according to Mueller's indictment of GRU officers. Trump's campaign framed these requests as jokes, but investigators found they aligned with a broader pattern of welcoming foreign interference. The Senate Intelligence Committee's bipartisan report described the campaign's openness to Russian assistance as representing a 'grave' counterintelligence threat. No criminal charges arose from these specific solicitations, though legal scholars argued they may have crossed statutory lines.

frozen_original.title: Trump Threatens to Sue Judges Who Rule Against Him
frozen_original.synopsis: By March 2025, Trump had publicly threatened on multiple occasions to sue, investigate, or otherwise retaliate against federal judges who issued rulings blocking his executive orders or finding his actions unconstitutional. The threats included social media posts identifying specific judges by name and calling for their impeachment, investigation, or removal. The intimidation campaign was seen as an attempt to chill judicial review of presidential actions by making the personal cost of adverse rulings prohibitively high — a core tactic of authoritarian capture of the judiciary.

proposed_title: Executive Order creates Schedule Policy/Career; OPM finalizes implementing rule in 2026
proposed_description_short: Executive Order creates Schedule Policy/Career; OPM finalizes implementing rule in 2026
proposed_description_medium: Executive Order 14171 established Schedule Policy/Career on January 20, 2025, replacing the earlier Schedule F label. OPM finalized an implementing rule in 2026 and issued later implementation guidance. The sources do not support the frozen claim that Russell Vought implemented Schedule F in February 2025; the order, final rule, and agency implementation occurred at different times.
proposed_description_long:
On January 20, 2025, Executive Order 14171 established Schedule Policy/Career, a category for certain policy-influencing career positions. The order revived the mechanism previously known as Schedule F under a different name. The Office of Personnel Management later finalized a rule to implement Schedule Policy/Career and issued guidance to agencies, with the final rule announced in 2026. These are distinct steps: the presidential order established the category, and later OPM action set out implementation details.

The frozen claim says Russell Vought's OMB implemented Schedule F in February 2025. The sources reviewed do not support that timing or description. The rulemaking had not been finalized then, and the 2025 executive order used the Schedule Policy/Career name. The corrected claim should distinguish the January 2025 executive order from OPM's 2026 final rule and subsequent agency guidance. It should not imply that every career civil servant was moved into the category or became automatically fireable.

frozen_original.synopsis: OMB Director Russell Vought implemented Schedule F, reclassifying tens of thousands of career civil servants whose work touches on policy as political appointees who can be fired at will without civil service protections. Good government organizations described Schedule F as the most sweeping attack on the nonpartisan federal workforce since the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883 created merit-based government employment.

The category affects career employees whose work involves policy, but the supplied correction emphasizes that they remain career employees selected through merit procedures. The key change is that covered positions lose some removal protections that apply to most competitive-service staff, giving agencies greater ability to remove employees in those roles. The distinction between career status and job protections matters for evaluating how the rule changes the civil service: employees remain in the merit system but face reduced safeguards. This entry uses the corrected dates and scope, replacing the earlier claim that Schedule F was implemented in February 2025 and that tens of thousands of workers became political appointees. The sources do not establish how many employees will ultimately be designated.
